title: Obtain Capabilities: Tool
summary: This sub-technique covers acquiring legitimate software tools for malicious use. The defining property is intent, not capability: the software was written for administration, testing, or remote management, and the adversary simply points it at a victim. Familiar examples include remote execution and service management utilities, network scanners, and commercial adversary simulation platforms. Acquisition looks like ordinary procurement, so it rarely appears suspicious in isolation. Adversaries download free utilities, buy commercial licences, crack trial builds, or steal licences and installers from other parties. A notable behaviour under this sub-technique is pre-deployment testing, where the tool or a payload is run against commercial antivirus and endpoint detection and response products to see which controls fire and to tune before a real operation. The defender problem is that the same binary appears in both benign and malicious activity, so a name or hash alert is almost useless on its own. The workable signal is context and pattern: which account ran it, from which host, against how many targets, at what hour, and whether an equivalent management platform was already in use. Remote execution utilities that copy a service binary to a remote host and start it leave service creation records and administrative share access, which together are far more telling than the tool name by itself.

beginner.definition: A tool is normal software used for a harmful purpose. Unlike malware, it was built to be helpful. Attackers buy it, download it free, or steal a licence, then use it to break into systems.
beginner.whyItMatters: These tools are already trusted and signed, so security software may allow them. Blocking a popular administration tool usually breaks real work too. That is why you need to judge each use by its context rather than by the tool itself.
howItWorks: The attacker picks a tool that does the job, such as running commands on remote machines.
They download it free, buy a licence, use a cracked trial, or steal a copy.
They test it against antivirus and endpoint detection tools to see what alarms.
They adjust settings or the payload until the tool passes their checks.
They use it inside the victim network to run commands and move between computers.
The traces look like administration, so defenders must compare against normal baselines.
beginner.example: A warehouse forklift is a legitimate machine that moves pallets. A thief can use the same forklift to load a van at night. Nothing about the forklift is criminal and it is not malware. What matters is who was driving it, which gate they used, and why the loading happened at three in the morning.
takeaways: A trusted tool used wrongly looks normal until you check the context.
Attackers test tools against security products before using them for real.
Baseline which administrators use which tools, on which hosts, and when.

objectives: Explain how a legitimate tool differs from malware in intent and detection.
Describe the ways adversaries obtain tools, including licence theft and cracked trials.
Explain why adversaries evaluate tools against endpoint security products.
Identify the logs that show remote execution tool usage in your environment.
Describe how to baseline legitimate administrative tool use to expose misuse.
